title: Children and rehat
hook: the code says amrit may be taken when one is old enough to understand

segments.voice: Yesterday, coming back after a lapse: a letter of leaving, torn up. Your line was you can return. Which habit did you pick up again, without a speech? Day one thousand two hundred ninety-six.

A small boy in a gurdwara sits beside his father with a tiny patka on his head, the knot slightly crooked. During the Ardas he stands when everyone stands, a beat late, and folds his hands because his father's hands are folded. He knows some of the words. He doesn't yet know what most of them mean. Is he keeping the rehat? Is he a Sikh yet? Or is he something in between, a learner who hasn't been asked the big question? The Sikh code has an answer about when that question gets asked, and it's not a number on a birthday card. That's today.
screen: `A CROOKED KNOT, A LATE STAND.` → `HE KNOWS THE WORDS, NOT YET THE MEANING.` → `WHEN DOES THE QUESTION GET ASKED?`

segments.voice: Begin with the line the hook points to. In the Rehat Maryada's section on amrit, the code says, in paraphrase, that the one being initiated should not be very young, and should have reached an age of understanding. Notice what it doesn't say. It doesn't set an age. There's no number in that line. The measure is understanding. Why? Think back to what the initiate is told at amrit: the daily banis, the five articles, the four things never to do. Those are promises. A promise only means something when the person making it knows what's being promised. So amrit waits for that. But waiting is not the same as leaving the child outside. Earlier in this block we met the naming ceremony, where a hukam is taken from the Guru Granth Sahib and the child's name begins with the first letter of that hymn. From the start, the child is brought into the Guru's presence. In families who keep the code, a child's hair is left uncut long before any vow, and the child grows up hearing Japji in the morning and Kirtan Sohila at night, sitting cross-legged in the langar line. That's how a child gets to understanding: not by being told the rules all at once, but by living inside them first. Some families teach Gurmukhi, the script of the Granth, so the child can read the hymns for themselves. And there's a quiet respect in this. The code doesn't take the choice away from the child by making it for them too early. It prepares the ground, and then it waits for the child to step forward on their own.
screen: `THE CODE: OLD ENOUGH TO UNDERSTAND.` · `NO NUMBER, ONLY UNDERSTANDING.` · `NAMED BEFORE THE GURU, RAISED INSIDE.` · then, large: `THE GROUND PREPARED, THE CHOICE KEPT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: explain one rule to a child. If there's a child in your life, think of one rule you keep, any rule, and how you'd explain it to them in two sentences, without saying because I said so. If there isn't, picture the child you once were, and explain it to them. Find the simplest true reason. Say it to yourself once. Then sit, breathe, and notice whether finding the simple reason changed how you hold the rule yourself. The bell holds the time.

Children and rehat. The Sikh code says amrit is not for the very young: one should be old enough to understand. Until then, children are named before the Guru and raised inside the practice. Today's word.

Your line: when they understand. Today, before you ask someone to keep a promise or follow a rule, check once that they actually understand what you're asking. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: Sikh children are named in the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib and raised with the daily prayers; the Rehat Maryada says amrit should be taken when one is old enough to understand, without setting an age.

trapdoor: what you thought: children in religious families are signed up from birth.
what it means: in the Sikh code, amrit waits until a person is old enough to understand.
what a scholar hears: the code gives no age, only understanding, so the vow stays the person's own choice, while naming and daily prayer raise the child inside the faith.

notes: The code's line on the age of initiates ('should not be of very tender age; should have attained a plausible degree of discretion' in common English renderings) is paraphrased as 'not very young, old enough to understand'. Please confirm.
Naming: the first letter of the hukam taken at the naming becomes the first letter of the child's name; please confirm wording.

'In families who keep the code, a child's hair is often left uncut' and 'some families teach Gurmukhi' are softened generalizations; the code also speaks of keeping children's hair intact and of Sikhs learning Gurmukhi. Please confirm what the code says directly and whether to cite it.
The phrase 'the child grows up hearing Japji in the morning and Kirtan Sohila at night' describes a household that keeps the daily banis; please confirm.
